beginner: Radish is one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes it a great first crop. The big seeds sprout strongly without soaking, need only a couple of dark days, and are usually ready in about a week. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish. The named kinds mostly just differ in color: Daikon has white stems and the most bite, China Rose and Red Arrow have pink stems and milder flavor, and Rambo and Sango have striking purple stems. You grow them all the same way. One safety rule for any microgreen: never grow them from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.
seasoned: Radish is among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short blackout, and finishes in roughly a week. The signature flavor is the peppery, pungent bite radish is known for, and it is described in extension trials as nutty and spicy. Named types differ mostly in stem color rather than growing method: white-stemmed Daikon runs strongest in spice, pink-stemmed China Rose and Red Arrow are milder and colorful, and purple Rambo or Sango are grown chiefly for their deep color. All are handled identically. Never grow microgreens from solanaceous seed (tomato, pepper, eggplant), whose seedlings carry alkaloids and are not safe to eat raw.

beginner: To always have radish microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow fast and indoors, you can keep this going all year.
seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Radish's roughly one-week cycle makes it easy to keep a rolling supply going. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.

beginner: Radish microgreens are baby radish plants that you harvest very young, about a week after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. They are one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes them a great first crop: the big seeds sprout strongly without any soaking, need only a day or two in the dark, and are usually ready in about 7 to 12 days. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish, and different kinds have white, pink, or purple stems. You grow them indoors all year with the same steps every time: scatter seeds thickly, cover the tray to keep it dark for a couple of days while they sprout, move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
seasoned: Radish microgreens are the young seedlings of the radish (Raphanus sativus), a brassica, harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage roughly a week after sowing. They are among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short dark blackout, and finishes in about 7 to 12 days. The flavor is a distinct peppery, pungent radish bite, and named types range from white-stemmed Daikon through pink China Rose and Red Arrow to deep-purple Rambo and Sango for color. They are grown indoors year-round in the same short cycle every time: a dense even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a brief blackout to even the stand, then light to green up, then a single cut. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the tray grows identically on any windowsill.

beginner: Your radish microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and the first true leaf is just showing, usually about a week after sowing (radish is fast). Snip them just above the medium with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.
seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically about 7 to 12 days from sowing and often around a week, since radish is one of the fastest microgreens. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
